reading.rtitle: The Kitchen at Four in the Morning
paras: A song has about three minutes and it cannot afford a paragraph of explanation, so it does something a novel almost never has to do: it drops you inside a scene that is already running. The rain was falling. She was standing in the kitchen with her coat still on. Nothing has been explained, and yet you know the time of night, the temperature and roughly how the conversation is going to go. That is what the continuous form is for in a lyric. It does not report an event; it opens a window on something already in progress, and the listener walks in halfway.

Then the events arrive, and they arrive in the past simple, one after another, like beats. She put the keys on the table. He asked where she had been. She did not answer. Each of those is finished, and the finished form is what moves a story forward. The two tenses do completely different jobs, and a good verse uses both in the same breath: while the radio was playing in the other room, he said the one sentence he could not take back. The background keeps running; the event lands on top of it.

The third tool is what the words refuse to do. A plain line such as she put the keys on the table hints at everything and states nothing. There is no adjective, no feeling named, and that is exactly why it works: the listener supplies the feeling, and a feeling you supplied yourself is stronger than one you were handed. The best lyrics are full of these images and almost empty of explanation. The narrator is not the writer either, which is a freedom beginners forget: the person speaking in the song can know less than you do, or lie.

And then, usually near the end, something turns. One line arrives and every line before it means something slightly different. The coat was never taken off, because she was never staying. That is the twist, and it is the reason the song unfolds instead of simply ending. Done well, it leaves the listener somewhere bittersweet, which is the emotional address where most memorable songs live: the happy version and the sad version of the same three minutes, arriving at the same second.

choices: To teach the grammar rules of the past tenses in general English.
To show the three things a lyric does with time and detail, and why they work.
To argue that songs are better than novels at telling stories.

items.situation: Open a scene: say what the weather was doing and what somebody was doing, at the same time.
tips: The rain was falling and she was standing in the doorway.
Two background actions running together: was / were plus -ing.

items.situation: Now put one finished event on top of that background.
tips: While the rain was falling, the phone rang.
The background is continuous, the event is past simple. That is the whole machine.

items.situation: Describe three finished actions in a row, with no feelings named.
tips: She put the keys on the table, sat down and did not say anything.
Plain past simple, one after another. The listener supplies the feeling.

items.situation: Give a detail that hints at something without stating it.
tips: She was still wearing her coat.
No adjective, no emotion word. The image does the work.

items.situation: Now add a twist: one line that changes what everything before it meant.
tips: She was still wearing her coat, because she was never staying.
The twist is a reveal, not a surprise. It re-reads the scene for you.

items.situation: Describe the opening of a song you know well, using both past forms.
tips: The narrator was driving home and the radio was on, and then he saw the house.
Background in the continuous, the event that starts the story in the simple.

listenings.text: I get sent a lot of first verses, and almost all of them have the same problem. They start with a feeling. I was so lost, I was broken, I did not know who I was any more. And I understand why, because that is the true thing, that is what the song is about. But a feeling is the conclusion, and you are giving me the conclusion in line one, so there is nothing left for me to do. Try this instead. Take the same verse and remove every word that names an emotion. What is left is usually a room, a time and an object, and those three things are the entire craft. The best opening line I read last year was six words long: the car was still running outside. Nobody said afraid. Nobody said leaving. And every single person who heard it knew both.

The twist is the most misunderstood thing in songwriting, because people hear the word and they think of a surprise ending, and that is not it at all. A surprise takes something away from you. A twist gives you something back. The difference is whether the line was available from the beginning. If I tell you at the end that the whole thing was a dream, you feel cheated, because there was nothing in the first two verses that could have told you. But if the coat was mentioned in verse one, and in the last line you find out she never took it off, you do not feel cheated. You feel clever, and you go back and listen again. That second listen is the entire commercial value of a twist. So here is the test I use. Write your last line first. Then go back into verse one and leave one small object there that makes the last line inevitable. If you cannot find the object, you do not have a twist. You have an ending.

extra_audio.text: Pedro says the verse sets a scene: the rain was falling and she was standing in the kitchen. Then he points out the events, in the past simple: she put the keys on the table and he asked where she had been. He notes that the lines are plain, with no emotion named anywhere. He says the images hint at everything and state nothing. He explains that the twist in the last line changes what came before it. Then he asks the other person what they noticed first.
